Date: 2026-10-25
By: Van
Soul Addey
The Nigeria Data Protection
Commission (NDPC) has called for stronger data governance, algorithmic
transparency and privacy-by-design in the development and regulation of
frontier artificial intelligence (AI), warning that uncurated data pipelines
used for advanced foundation models could expose the national digital ecosystem
to cyber exploitation and mass disinformation.
The Commission made the call
at a Stakeholders’ Consultation on Frontier AI hosted by NITHUB, the University
of Lagos and the Tech Governance Project.
The NDPC’s National
Commissioner and Chief Executive Officer, Dr Vincent Olatunji, was represented
at the consultation by Abubakar Mahmud, an officer from the Commission’s IT and
Cybersecurity Department, who delivered the keynote remarks.
Mahmud highlighted the
vulnerabilities associated with using uncurated data pipelines for advanced
foundation models and stressed the importance of safeguards to address emerging
risks.
He also emphasised that the
Nigeria Data Protection Act, 2023, mandates strict data minimisation and
algorithmic transparency.
Mahmud advocated for the
integration of ISO/IEC 42001:2023 standards into Nigeria’s upcoming AI
Regulatory Sandboxing Platform to embed privacy-by-design and accountability
from inception.
He said the Commission
remained committed to a multi-stakeholder alliance involving government,
academia, industry and civil society through proactive co-creation, regional
harmonisation across Africa and collaborative alignment with international
standards.
He assured delegates that
collective efforts would help safeguard sovereign digital assets and foster an
AI ecosystem where Nigerian technology stands as a global beacon of trust and
safety.
The consultation explored
the paradigm shift brought about by highly capable general-purpose foundation
models, highlighting the transformative possibilities of frontier AI for
national development while ensuring that robust data governance is established
to mitigate emerging systemic risks.

Source：Shutterstock
TSMC is exploring alternatives to rare-earth magnets used in factory equipment, according to Reuters. The move highlights a vulnerability in Taiwan's semiconductor supply chain—even though chipmaking itself consumes relatively little rare-earth material.

Why TSMC Is Seeking Rare-Earth-Free Equipment as China Tightens Its Grip
By CommonWealth Magazine
web only
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), the world's largest contract chipmaker, is exploring ways to reduce its reliance on rare-earth components in factory equipment as China's export controls raise concerns about potential disruptions to advanced semiconductor production.
According to an October 22 Reuters exclusive, three people familiar with the matter said TSMC had asked suppliers about using motors that do not require rare-earth magnets in its factory automation equipment.
The discussions remain preliminary, and no broad replacement program has been reported. TSMC did not comment on the Reuters report.
The development raises an important question: If rare earths account for only a small portion of the materials used in semiconductor manufacturing, why is the world's most advanced chipmaker looking for alternatives?
The answer lies in the distinction between the materials used to manufacture chips and the machinery needed to keep semiconductor factories operating.
China's rare-earth restrictions may have a limited direct impact on semiconductor production, but they can still create vulnerabilities in the equipment supply chain.
How does China's control of rare earths affect semiconductor equipment?
China's influence over the rare-earth supply chain extends well beyond mining.
In an earlier CommonWealth investigation into China's rare-earth leverage, industry experts explained that China's strongest position lies in refining and processing, where it controls much of the world's capacity.
Even rare-earth minerals extracted outside China may still pass through Chinese processing facilities before becoming usable industrial materials.
This creates dependencies across several stages of production.
A semiconductor equipment supplier may source motors from another country, while the magnets inside those motors rely on materials refined or manufactured in China.
Restrictions on rare-earth exports can therefore affect international manufacturers that do not purchase their raw materials directly from Chinese mining companies.
For chipmakers, the potential consequences extend beyond higher component prices.
A shortage of qualified replacement parts could complicate equipment maintenance, expansion, or procurement.
However, the scale of that risk depends on which components are affected, how much inventory suppliers maintain, and whether alternative products meet semiconductor manufacturing requirements.
Not every rare-earth restriction has the same impact on every piece of equipment.
Can TSMC replace rare-earth magnets with alternative motors?
Potentially, but replacing a component in a semiconductor manufacturing environment is not simply a matter of purchasing a different motor.
Rare-earth permanent magnets are widely used because they can provide strong magnetic performance in compact, efficient designs.
Alternative motor technologies may avoid certain rare-earth materials, but their suitability depends on the equipment's requirements.
Engineers must consider factors such as size, precision, energy efficiency, heat generation, reliability, and compatibility with existing machinery.
In semiconductor manufacturing, changes to equipment may also require extensive qualification before deployment.
Taiwan already has companies developing technologies that could help reduce reliance on rare-earth materials.
CommonWealth reported in May 2025 that Taiwanese manufacturer TECO Electric had developed motors that do not require rare earths.
Such technologies demonstrate that alternatives exist, although they do not establish that any particular motor is qualified for use in TSMC's semiconductor equipment.
Reuters did not identify which suppliers TSMC had approached or specify which alternative motor technologies were under consideration.
It remains unclear whether the company's discussions will lead to widespread equipment changes.
Taiwan wants to produce half its own rare-earth needs by 2030
Alongside the industry's search for substitutes, Taiwan is pursuing a separate strategy: developing domestic rare-earth processing and production capabilities.
On October 24, Taiwan's Industrial Technology Research Institute (ITRI) disclosed plans to establish a demonstration facility capable of producing approximately 500 metric tons of rare-earth materials annually by the end of 2030.
According to Taiwan's Central News Agency, ITRI President Chang Pei-zen said the proposed output could meet about half of Taiwan's domestic demand.
The institute currently operates an experimental production line with an annual output of approximately five metric tons.
Reaching the proposed target would therefore require increasing output by roughly 100 times.
ITRI aims to complete construction of the demonstration facility by the end of 2028, then refine production processes and work toward the 2030 capacity target.
The project remains in the planning stage.
Funding arrangements, potential government support for private investors, and the commercial model have not been finalized.
The technical challenge is also substantial.
Rare-earth elements have similar chemical properties, making separation and purification complex. Producing high-quality materials at industrial scale requires specialized processes, equipment, and expertise.
The proposed facility represents an effort to build capabilities that Taiwan currently lacks at scale, rather than an immediate solution to the semiconductor industry's supply-chain concerns.
It is also important to distinguish the new production target from earlier, narrower estimates of rare-earth demand for specific industrial uses. The announced 500-ton capacity goal and the estimate that it could meet half of domestic demand refer to a broader planned production scope; they should not be directly compared with figures for semiconductor-specific consumption.
Can Taiwan reduce its dependence on China's rare earths?
Taiwan has several potential ways to reduce its exposure to Chinese rare-earth supply restrictions.
One is to diversify sources of raw materials and processed products.
Another is to develop local separation, refining, recycling, and magnet-production capabilities.
A third is technological substitution, including motors and equipment designed to operate without certain rare-earth materials.
Each approach addresses a different part of the supply chain.
Diversification can reduce dependence on a single supplier or country, but alternative suppliers may still rely on Chinese processing.
Domestic production could provide greater control over selected materials, but building industrial-scale capacity takes time and investment.
Substitution could eliminate the need for certain restricted materials altogether, although alternatives must meet the demanding technical standards of their intended applications.
Taiwan is also working with international partners to strengthen critical-mineral supply chains.
Reuters reported that the United States has expressed interest in ITRI's rare-earth development efforts as Washington and Taipei explore ways to diversify supply and processing capacity.
For Taiwan's semiconductor industry, the goal is not necessarily to replace every imported rare-earth component.
It is to ensure that a restriction affecting a relatively small but critical component does not become a bottleneck for an industry central to the global technology economy.
FAQs
Does TSMC use rare earths?
Rare-earth materials are used in certain industrial equipment components, including permanent magnets in motors. Reuters reported that TSMC is exploring motors that do not require rare-earth components for factory automation equipment.
Why is TSMC looking for rare-earth-free equipment?
According to Reuters, TSMC has consulted suppliers about alternatives as a precaution against potential disruptions caused by China's rare-earth export controls. The discussions are preliminary.
Could China stop Taiwan from making advanced chips by restricting rare earths?
China's controls could create equipment supply-chain risks, but there is no evidence that they have stopped TSMC's advanced chip production. The impact depends on affected components, inventories, alternative suppliers, and equipment qualification.
Can semiconductor factories operate without rare-earth magnets?
Some alternative motor technologies do not require rare-earth magnets. However, whether they can replace existing components depends on the equipment's technical and operational requirements.
Does Taiwan produce its own rare earths?
Taiwan has experimental rare-earth production and processing capabilities. ITRI is planning a demonstration facility targeting annual output of 500 metric tons by the end of 2030, but the project has not yet reached commercial scale.
Why does China dominate the rare-earth supply chain?
China has a particularly strong position in rare-earth processing and refining, not just mining. This makes international manufacturers dependent on Chinese supply-chain stages even when raw materials originate elsewhere.

TSMC's reported search for rare-earth-free equipment does not contradict earlier assessments that Taiwan's semiconductor industry has relatively limited direct demand for rare-earth materials.

articles.title: Elon Musk admits SpaceX restricted Starlink in Ukraine - Tech Digest
articles.summary: Elon Musk admits SpaceX restricted Starlink in Ukraine  Tech Digest
articles.full_text:
Tech billionaire Elon Musk has confirmed that his company, SpaceX, intentionally restricted the Starlink satellite internet service in Ukraine, citing violations of the company’s terms of service regarding military operations.
The admission follows a week-long disruption that severely hampered Ukraine’s defensive operations and military communications. The connectivity crisis emerged during a tense diplomatic standoff between Washington and Kyiv over Ukrainian strikes on Russian oil infrastructure.
US President Donald Trump stated he instructed Musk to restore the service, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy subsequently confirmed that connectivity across both Starlink and the military-grade Starshield network had returned to stable levels.
Writing on X, Musk defended the move, stating that using a civilian commercial service for offensive actions violated policy.
“Using Starlink, a civilian commercial service, for offensive drone strikes to kill people has never been allowed, nor should it be,” Musk wrote. “Ukraine’s military violated Starlink terms of service and used it for offensive drone strikes to kill people. That loophole was closed last week.”
Musk maintained that SpaceX has done more to support Ukraine than any private company on Earth since Russia’s full-scale invasion began. He also clarified that Starshield, the separate military counterpart, is controlled by the US government and operates under independent jurisdiction.
Ukrainian officials expressed bewilderment over Musk’s justification. Presidential adviser Serhii Beskrestnov pointed out that commercial Starlink terminals in Ukraine feature built-in speed restrictions and do not function over Russian territory, making it physically impossible to use them for deep-strike operations.
Military commanders reported that the throttling had interrupted missions and blinded drone operators, though defence officials confirmed that network speeds and stability have now been restored.

articles.title: Modders unlock hidden AI performance on NVIDIA RTX 20, 30 and 40 series GPUs, with up to 2× tensor throughput - VideoCardz.com
articles.summary: Modders unlock hidden AI performance on NVIDIA RTX 20, 30 and 40 series GPUs, with up to 2× tensor throughput  VideoCardz.comNvidia RTX 20, 30, and 40-series GPUs hacked to remove a half-speed AI throttle — firmware exploit doubles RTX 4090's peak tensor rate, lifts RTX 3090 Ti matrix math up to 80%  Tom's HardwareGeForce Unlocked: Modders Boost RTX 20, RTX 30, and RTX 40 Compute Performance by Up to 2x  TechPowerUpModders Unlock GeForce RTX 20, 30 And 40 GPUs For U...
articles.full_text:
NVIDIA’s older GeForce GPUs have restricted AI performance, modders are removing the limits
Modders have found ways to remove NVIDIA’s compute performance restrictions on several generations of GeForce graphics cards. What started with the RTX 3090 series has now expanded to RTX 40 models and even the older RTX 2080 Ti.
The modifications can nearly double the throughput of certain Tensor Core operations without changing the hardware or flashing a new VBIOS. However, this does not mean twice the gaming performance, and the GeForce RTX 50 Blackwell series has yet to receive a confirmed working unlock.
How it started
The research builds on earlier attempts to unlock restricted compute capabilities on NVIDIA CMP mining GPUs. Developer Zagitta adapted these techniques for GeForce RTX 30 cards through the open-source GPU-Unlock project, while work involving TOTORONG’s firmware payload extended support to the Ada architecture.
Instead of modifying graphics drivers, the tools change low-level GPU configuration registers before the NVIDIA driver loads, removing limits on the rate at which certain Tensor Core instructions can be issued. The changes are temporary and are cleared when the GPU loses power.
Up to twice the tensor throughput, but not in games
The reported results are substantial in specific compute tests. An RTX 3090 Ti increased BF16 matrix multiplication performance from 87.5 to 157.4 TFLOPS, while an RTX 4090 doubled its measured FP16 Tensor Core instruction throughput from 165.6 to 331.6 TFLOPS. KohakuBlueleaf has also demonstrated an RTX 2080 Ti reaching 111 TFLOPS, compared with 59.9 TFLOPS before the unlock. That particular card was already physically modified with 22GB of VRAM, which is unrelated to the software unlock. Successful tests have also been reported on RTX 3060, RTX 3070, RTX 3080 and selected RTX 40 models, although support is not yet validated across every GPU variant.
These modifications primarily affect FP16 and BF16 operations with FP32 accumulation, alongside certain TF32 and FP8 workloads on supported architectures. They can accelerate AI tasks involving matrix multiplication, including LLM prompt processing and some image-generation workloads.
However, actual gains depend on the software being used. RTX 3090 reports show LLM prompt-processing improvements of roughly 14% to 36%, while token generation remains largely unchanged because it is often limited by memory bandwidth. Gaming performance is unaffected by these specific unlocks. Most projects currently target Linux, although experimental Windows implementations are also available. They are not risk-free, and unsupported configurations may fail to boot.
Could this affect used GeForce prices?
Some users are already asking NVIDIA to officially remove these restrictions from older GeForce products, many of which are no longer manufactured. That would benefit owners using their existing GPUs for AI workloads, but it raises another question for gamers. Cards such as the RTX 3090 and RTX 4090 already attract AI buyers because of their 24GB memory capacity, and improving their compute performance could make them even more attractive on the second-hand market.
So perhaps asking NVIDIA to remove these restrictions is the right call, just not at the best time. It’s hard to argue against unlocking performance on GPUs that are no longer in production and, in most cases, already out of warranty. But the GPU market is hardly in good shape right now, and making older GeForce cards more attractive to AI users could make things even worse for gamers. But can it really get any worse?
Source: RTX 30 Unlock (GPU-Unlock), RTX 40 Unlock (GPU-Unlock-Ada), RTX 20 Unlock (Turing Unlock)

articles.title: From Ukraine’s Starlink dependency to India’s NavIC challenge—lessons in space sovereignty - ThePrint
articles.summary: From Ukraine’s Starlink dependency to India’s NavIC challenge—lessons in space sovereignty  ThePrint
articles.full_text:
In the last few weeks, Ukrainian military operations have faced significant disruption after certain restrictions were imposed on services offered by Starlink and its military-oriented counterpart, Starshield. Reports indicated that connections became unreliable or failed for platforms moving faster than approximately 160 km/h. This limit severely impacted drone interceptions, communications, and other air defence tasks. Ukrainian officials, including President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, stated that the limits hampered Ukraine’s ability to intercept Russian attack drones. Reports also indicated that offensive drone operations had been cancelled. SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk acknowledged restrictions on Starlink access in Ukraine. He accused Ukraine’s military of exploiting the satellite internet service for offensive drone strikes, and warned that a complete shutdown of SpaceX services could cause Ukraine’s front line to collapse.
Much political activity followed, including personal intervention by President Trump. Eventually, the restrictions were lifted by 24 October. The episode revealed a key vulnerability that also served as a centre of gravity (CoG). It highlighted the dangers of operational dependence on a privately controlled satellite system that relies on the operator’s willingness to act in a compliant and friendly manner. When Starlink and Starshield were withheld, Ukraine appeared defenceless.
There are lessons for India in this episode that must be carefully extracted through an analysis of the events. The episode comes against the backdrop of recent controversy surrounding Elon Musk’s accusations that “certain oligarchs were blocking Starlink’s satellite communication services in India”, followed by denials from the Indian government. This makes space sovereignty even more significant.
We start by understanding the basics.
Starlink and Starshield
Starlink is SpaceX’s commercial low-Earth orbit (LEO) broadband constellation. It provides high-speed, low-latency internet (typically 20–40 ms) to users on a paid basis. Its typical user base comprises civilians, enterprises, maritime vessels, aviation companies and government agencies, including the military. The service has near-global coverage and is delivered through an array of ground stations and compact phased-array user terminals. As of late 2026, the constellation had well over 11,000 active satellites. Services are sold directly by SpaceX under commercial terms.
Starshield is SpaceX’s national-security offering for government and military customers. It provides secure communications, Earth observation capabilities, and hosted payloads with enhanced encryption. User terminals are dedicated, rugged and more expensive. Service levels, prioritisation, and operational limits are governed by contracts. The United States is the primary customer, with some services offered to US allies such as the United Kingdom.
The two systems share substantial infrastructure. Starshield communications primarily use the Starlink satellite constellation as a backbone. The systems also share launch capability, engineering, inter-satellite laser links, and ground stations, including terrestrial gateways. Where required, dedicated terminals and separate network gateways provide segregation, higher-assurance cryptography, and different control authorities. Outages (or policy intervention) in one constellation can therefore affect both services. In short, the satellites and much of the ground architecture are common; the distinction lies in encryption, terminals, prioritisation, ownership of certain payloads, and who holds operational control.
Alternatives to Starlink
Several other LEO broadband constellations are in operation or at advanced stages of deployment. Eutelsat OneWeb operates a constellation of several hundred satellites focused on enterprise, government, and mobility markets. Eutelsat works closely with Indian companies such as Nelco Limited (a satellite communication service provider belonging to the Tata Group) and Bharti Airtel.
Similarly, Amazon Leo (formerly Project Kuiper) has launched hundreds of satellites and is scaling production, targeting commercial service in multiple markets. China’s Guowang and Qianfan (Thousand Sails) projects aim to establish large national constellations for broadband and strategic connectivity. Europe’s IRIS² is a planned sovereign multi-orbit system.
Compared with Starlink, these systems generally offer lower peak capacity and slower deployment timelines. In most cases, they lack the same density of inter-satellite laser links. None currently matches Starlink’s combination of scale, global coverage, and demonstrated low latency for mobile users, though several are progressing rapidly.
Russia’s Rassvet effort
Russia’s Bureau 1440 is developing the Rassvet (Russian for dawn or daybreak) LEO broadband constellation as a domestic alternative. By late October 2026, 38 satellites had been launched across two batches. Although several satellites experienced difficulties raising their orbits, plans remain in place to launch 156 satellites by the end of 2026, with partial commercial service expected by late 2027. The long-term target is 900 satellites. The system is intended to support broadband and, eventually, 5G non-terrestrial network features. It remains far from Starlink’s scale or maturity and has shown early reliability issues.
Chinese capabilities
China is building two major Starlink-style LEO broadband constellations: Guowang (China SatNet), targeting roughly 13,000 satellites, and Qianfan (Thousand Sails/G60), aiming for up to about 15,000 satellites. As of late October 2026, Guowang had around 220 satellites in orbit, while Qianfan had roughly 250. Both began deployment in 2024, use multiple orbital shells, and remain well behind their 2026 targets. Challenges involving launch cadence and unspecified technical constraints have delayed deployment. They are intended to deliver sovereign, high-capacity connectivity for civilian, government, and military use. Combined, they have fewer than 500 satellites in orbit, compared with Starlink’s more than 11,000 working spacecraft. China has barred consumer Starlink access and is accelerating domestic launches. However, both programmes are still at an early stage, with service maturity, density, latency, and global reach yet to match the levels achieved by Starlink.
One interesting feature of Chinese efforts has been the early recognition of dependence on global navigation satellite systems (GNSS) and attempts to create a terrestrial backup. China operates the BeiDou Navigation Satellite System, a fully independent global GNSS with regional enhancements. It provides positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) services worldwide and is integrated into Chinese military and civilian infrastructure. In a unique approach, China has complemented its GNSS with a terrestrial system. China has created and expanded a national enhanced Loran (eLoran) terrestrial network. Ground stations provide high-power, low-frequency timing and positioning signals that are far more resistant to jamming and GNSS denial attempts. The system is designed as a backup and complement to satellite navigation, with demonstrated timing accuracy improvements.
GNSS dependency
Virtually all current LEO broadband user terminals (including those discussed above) require accurate knowledge of their own position to function effectively. In standard designs, this information is obtained from GNSS receivers (GPS, BeiDou, Galileo or GLONASS). Without it, terminals cannot form precise beams or maintain reliable links, especially while moving. Starlink has demonstrated a GNSS-independent positioning capability derived from its own constellation; however, equivalent capabilities are not widely available. Most other systems, including planned Russian and Chinese broadband constellations and the systems proposed for India, have not publicly demonstrated equivalent independent modes. Therefore, access to GNSS signals remains a key dependency and a vulnerability.

The Indian situation
India has licensed several operators for satellite broadband but has not yet authorised commercial LEO consumer services. The final decision is pending spectrum allocation and security clearances. Reliance Jio holds a Global Mobile Personal Communications by Satellite (GMPCS) licence. At the recently concluded India Mobile Congress (IMC) 2026 in New Delhi, Jio displayed the banner reading ‘Sovereign Satellite Connectivity’. The company has proposed a constellation of around 1,600 low-Earth orbit (LEO) satellites and 23 ground stations across India. The plan targets broadband and direct-to-device services, with a test flight around September 2027, several hundred satellites by 2030, and full deployment later. Bharti-backed Eutelsat OneWeb is further advanced in securing regulatory approvals and has partnered with Tata Group companies for ground infrastructure. Starlink and Amazon Leo are also in the regulatory pipeline.
All of these systems will require reliable PNT for their operation. Until Navigation with Indian Constellation (NavIC) regains the capability to provide PNT services, Indian terminals will depend on GPS, GLONASS, BeiDou, or Galileo for positioning, navigation and timing.
NavIC is India’s regional GNSS. Ageing satellites, atomic-clock failures, and the loss of NVS-02 due to a propulsion problem left the constellation short of the minimum of four satellites needed for reliable PNT services. ISRO has scheduled the launch of NVS-03 on 30 October aboard GSLV Mk II to help restore its capability, with further NVS satellites planned for subsequent launches.

articles.summary: Why do Japanese people still turn their backs on Chinese electric vehicles?  Vietnam.vn
articles.full_text:
BYD is growing in Japan, but its passenger car market share is still below 0.1%. Developing the RACCO electric vehicle specifically for this market shows the Chinese automaker must adapt to consumer habits, subsidy policies, and the long-standing advantages of domestic manufacturers.
In late July, BYD launched the RACCO compact electric vehicle in the Japanese market, targeting the kei car segment – a category of small cars suitable for daily commuting and accounting for the largest share of new car sales in the country. The RACCO was developed specifically according to Japanese kei car standards, rather than simply importing an existing model from another market. This is a different approach compared to competing with global electric vehicle models previously.
However, optimizing products for the local market only solves part of the problem. BYD still faces competition from Japanese brands that possess extensive sales networks, long-standing reputations, and deep understanding of local customers.
According to Toyokeizai , BYD registered 3,742 passenger cars in Japan in 2025. Compared to the total number of new cars sold (including kei cars) of approximately 4.57 million, BYD's share was less than 0.1%. In the first half of 2026, the company registered an additional 2,334 vehicles, a 42.7% increase compared to the same period the previous year. Notably, the SEALION 6 Plug-in Hybrid (PHEV) SUV contributed 1,254 vehicles, accounting for more than half of the total registrations. This shows that BYD's growth in Japan is not solely based on pure electric vehicles.
Increased sales are a positive sign, but not enough to confirm that BYD has established a firm foothold. The company still needs to find a way to translate customers' initial curiosity into consistent sales in a market where purely electric vehicles (BEVs) are not as common as in China or Europe.
Invisible disadvantages from subsidy policies
A major obstacle for BYD is the highly specific product structure of the Japanese market. Hybrid vehicles (HEVs) are deeply entrenched, while family car buyers have too many reputable options from domestic brands. According to data from Toyokeizai , purely electric passenger cars (excluding kei cars) will only account for a mere 1.6% of the Japanese market in 2025. For those accustomed to driving hybrids from Toyota, Honda, or Nissan, switching to electric vehicles is not just a brand change, but a complete overhaul of their lifestyle, from charging infrastructure and driving range to operating costs.
The RACCO was created to appeal to this urban customer segment with its high-riding design, power-sliding doors on both sides, and a range of 210 km to 320 km depending on the version. The starting price is 2.145 million yen, with higher-end versions priced at 2.398 million and 2.497 million yen respectively.
You may also like
However, a lower list price than competitors doesn't necessarily mean a lower actual purchase cost. RACCO only receives a national subsidy of 150,000 yen, bringing the price of the basic version down to around 1.995 million yen. Meanwhile, the Nissan Sakura – a domestically produced electric kei – despite having a higher list price, receives a subsidy of up to 580,000 yen in 2026. Thanks to this, the price of the Sakura S version after the subsidy is only around 1.869 million yen, about 126,000 yen lower than RACCO. BYD's price advantage is completely reversed by the government's implicit protectionist policies through subsidies.
Japanese consumers are known for being discerning; they don't just look at the list price but consider a combination of factors: subsidies, features, range, and resale value. The RACCO has the advantage of power sliding doors and a 320 km range in the top-of-the-line version, but BYD will have to struggle to prove that these features justify the price difference compared to familiar Japanese models.
Furthermore, brand trust is also an invisible barrier. AlixPartners ' 2026 global automotive consumer survey indicated that 44% of respondents avoided Chinese brands, compared to only 17% for Japanese brands. Although this is global data, not just from Japan, it still reflects the image challenge that BYD must overcome. In a country with extremely high loyalty to domestic products like Japan, BYD cannot rely solely on technology or price; they need to demonstrate durability and after-sales service throughout the vehicle's lifecycle.
Kei cars: The ultimate test.
The kei car segment has a huge market share but is extremely difficult to penetrate. Kei cars are expected to account for approximately 34.5% of new car sales in Japan in fiscal year 2025. Major players like Suzuki and Daihatsu have a monopoly on this segment thanks to their extensive distribution networks reaching even rural areas and their deep understanding of customer needs.
BYD is working to close this gap. The company had 56 official stores by early August 2026 and aims to reach 100 outlets by the end of the year. RACCO has also initially attracted interest, receiving approximately 1,500 orders by the end of August.
However, the actual number of RACCO vehicles registered in August was only 81. BYD explained that the majority of deliveries were the basic RACCO 200 version, while the 300 Premium version (accounting for over 80% of orders) would not begin deliveries until the second half of September. This figure needs to be viewed realistically: Orders only reflect media hype, while the actual number of vehicles on the road is a measure of the company's supply chain capacity and cash flow. Sales trends in the following months will provide the clearest answer to whether RACCO will thrive in Japan.
You may also like
Many people often look to the success of BYD's electric bus segment in Japan (delivering over 500 vehicles, accounting for half of the electric bus market share by 2025) to set expectations for the passenger car segment. However, these two segments are completely different. Bus buyers are transportation companies, and their decisions are based on dry figures about operating costs (OPEX). Individual customers buying family cars, on the other hand, are heavily influenced by emotions, habits, convenience of maintenance, and brand trust.
BYD's challenge in Japan therefore leaves no room for shortcuts. RACCO shows it is proactively adapting, but expanding its market share will depend entirely on how it optimizes post-subsidy costs, establishes a dense network of repair shops, and convinces Japanese consumers to trust a foreign brand.

articles.summary: Microsoft Teams to Use AI for Detecting Phishing Attacks Using Teams Conversations  CyberSecurityNewsMicrosoft Teams to get AI-powered, context-aware phishing detection  BleepingComputerMicrosoft Teams to get AI protection against phishing and fraud  ComputerworldHow Microsoft Teams is tackling the growing threat of deepfakes  SpiceworksAI-powered phishing detection, third PHP2Shell bug, Quest medical breach  LinkedIn
articles.full_text:
Microsoft is preparing to add AI phishing detection to Microsoft Teams, using conversation context to spot scams that may contain no harmful links or attachments. The feature will focus mainly on first conversations with external contacts, where attackers can pose as trusted support staff and ask employees to share sensitive information.
Microsoft detailed the change in Message Center notice MC1519866, published on October 21, 2026. Targeted Release is scheduled to begin in early November and finish by mid-November. Worldwide general availability is expected to start in early December and finish by mid-December, rather than reaching every customer in November.
How Conversation Context Helps Detect Phishing
Traditional warning signs, such as suspicious links and infected files, are not always present in social engineering attacks. A message can instead build trust, claim an urgent account problem, and persuade someone to disclose a password or approve remote access.
Microsoft says the new capability will analyze conversation context to identify phishing, impersonation, social engineering, and deceptive intent. Its support guidance describes coverage for individual and group chats involving new external contacts across mobile, desktop, and web. Roadmap entry 575288 lists Android, iOS, Mac, desktop, and web support for the worldwide standard cloud.
The warning example accompanying the announcement shows an external account called “MOD Administrator” discussing permission problems before asking, “Can you share your credential first?” Teams displays a notice saying the message could be a phishing attempt. The example illustrates why the meaning of a conversation can matter even without a dangerous URL.
This addresses a familiar attack pattern. Cybersecurity News previously reported on attackers impersonating IT help desk staff through Teams, using convincing support requests to push users toward malware or remote access. Separate reporting described fake support operators abusing Quick Assist after contacting employees through external Teams accounts.
Microsoft says detection may initially run silently while it checks quality. Visible warnings may appear after that validation, so users should not expect every suspicious message to trigger an immediate banner during the rollout.
For most users, protection centers on external first-contact chats. Teams mobile users in China may also receive protection for conversations within their own organization, reflecting fraud patterns seen in that region. This is a specific extension, not a promise of universal internal chat scanning.
Microsoft states that the capability serves security purposes only. It is not intended for advertising, employee monitoring, productivity analysis, or conversation summaries. Customer message content is not retained by the detection system for model training or other secondary uses. That statement should not be read as a change to all existing Teams retention policies.
What Organizations Should Do
No new administrator configuration is required to enable the protection. However, Microsoft recommends reviewing guidance for unfamiliar external contacts and encouraging users to report suspicious activity or incorrect detections.
When a warning appears, employees should check the sender’s identity and email address through a trusted channel. Microsoft advises blocking and reporting confirmed phishing, while mistaken warnings can be reported as not a concern. Users should never share passwords, verification codes, financial details, or sensitive information through an unexpected support conversation.
The update adds another warning layer, but staff still need to independently verify unexpected support requests and report suspicious contacts, rather than treating the absence of a banner as proof of safety.

articles.title: Sunlight at night: US startup’s demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws criticism - The Guardian
articles.summary: Sunlight at night: US startup’s demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws criticism  The GuardianAn American startup wants to sell sunlight after dark. Who gets a say?  Phys.orgA Satellite Company Tested “Sunlight As A Service” — Without Astronomers’ Knowledge  Sky & TelescopeA rehearsal for space mirrors leaves California rescuers unconvinced  DarkSky InternationalMysterious Blinding Lights Near Mount Whitney Reveal Reflect Orbital Ground Test for ...
articles.full_text:
Locals in a rural area of California were recently startled to see dazzlingly bright light shining down from nearby mountains at night, illuminating a swathe of the desert below.
Unbeknown to them, the strange nocturnal illumination was the latest step in a company’s plan to erect thousands of giant mirrors in space to reflect sunlight on to the Earth during night-time.
The night-time light demonstration, near the town of Lone Pine in the Sierra Nevada region, was conducted by a US startup called Reflect Orbital, which has an almost sci-fi aim to launch 50,000 satellites into space in the next decade to illuminate parts of the world at night.
In July, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) approved Reflect Orbital’s proposal to launch an initial demonstration satellite next year, which will orbit the Earth and, via a 59ft-diameter mirror, reflect sunlight in 3-mile-wide beams in strengths from moonlight up to the brightness of the sun at noon.
The demonstration in California, undertaken earlier this month, showcased what this would look like on the ground, to the bewilderment of locals, one of whom called the lights “blinding”. Large mobile lights were erected near Mount Whitney, with Reflect Orbital comparing the radiance to that of a full moon.
This provided, the company said, a realistic simulation of one of the benefits of this technology: to help search-and-rescue teams and other emergency responders at night. Other planned uses include bathing crops in sunlight, replacing broken streetlights and even providing solar power for military operations, all summoned by the tap of a button on an app.
“Search-and-rescue teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who would use our technology,” said a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital, which partnered with a local search-and-rescue team for the demonstration.
“We’ll keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever we operate, and are excited to show how this technology can help save lives.”
A coalition of environmentalists and astronomers are far less excited about Reflect Orbital’s ambitions, however. These groups have criticized the company and the FCC for threatening a harmful change to the separation of night and day that will affect everything from people’s sleep to wildlife and the ability to see the stars from Earth.
“This is an idiotic project,” said Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney with Earthjustice, an environmental group. “There are a huge number of unresolved questions and significant potential impacts. Literally all of life on Earth evolved based on the rhythm of day and night and there is a ton of data showing that messing with this is not a good idea.”
“There needs to be some sort of discussion and analysis before we grant these people the right to fundamentally alter the night sky,” he added. “The proposal for 50,000 of these satellite mirrors is crazy and would really end the night sky as we know it.”
In August, four groups represented by Earthjustice asked the FCC to reconsider its approval, citing concerns that opening up the skies to mirrored satellites, which would ascend to about 400 miles (645km) above the Earth’s surface before reflecting light back, would cause a litany of problems.
Animals such as birds, insects and mammals rely on the reliable change between day and night to feed, shelter and mate, with any change to this being potentially disastrous for some species.
Astronomers, meanwhile, have complained that this night-time glare would worsen existing light pollution and spur an overall rush to add more satellites to orbit – Elon Musk’s SpaceX plans to place 1 million celestial datacenters around Earth – that will obscure the stars and cause more space debris that could descend as pollution back to our world.
There are also concerns that the scrambling of night and day will harm people’s health by disrupting their circadian rhythms as they sleep. Looking directly at the unusual glaring sunlight at night would also, much like doing so during a solar eclipse, harm people’s eyes.
Reflect Orbital has said its technology will actually aid the environment by boosting the energy output of solar panels when sunlight is pointed at them during night-time, thereby reducing reliance on fossil fuels.
But some climate scientists have warned against meddling with the amount of sun’s energy reaching Earth. Proposals for solar geoengineering, in which particles are sprayed into the atmosphere to deflect sunlight away from Earth instead of toward it, have also prompted fierce opposition.
“Global warming is happening because the Earth has a radiative imbalance due to the massive amounts of greenhouse gases we’ve dumped into the atmosphere,” said David Ho, a climate scientist at the University of Hawaii.
“Some people are promoting the already unhinged idea of installing space mirrors facing away from the Earth to reflect the sun’s energy in order to decrease global warming. Imagine wanting to turn those mirrors around so that the Earth gets hotter.”
Reflect Orbital said it has had “substantive discussions” with scientists and astronomers on the use of its technology so that areas such as astronomical sites, national parks and other wildlife-rich areas are avoided.
“We welcome oversight and want to play a role in shaping it,” a spokesperson said. “We believe it is our responsibility to work alongside governments, scientists and regulators rather than ahead of them.”

articles.title: Nvidia Could Exploit “Completely Legal” China Loophole Worth Billions. But It (Probably) Won’t. - TIKR.com
articles.summary: Nvidia Could Exploit “Completely Legal” China Loophole Worth Billions. But It (Probably) Won’t.  TIKR.com
articles.full_text:
Key Takeaways
- ByteDance, Alibaba and Tencent have reportedly ordered more than $35 billion of NVIDIA’s export-compliant chips, and export-control expert Chris McGuire says Chinese companies can also legally rent US-made AI compute from data centers abroad, or even in the US.
- NVIDIA probably won’t go after that rental demand, because it can’t make enough chips as it is and its guidance already assumes no China data center revenue.
- The risk is that no one has measured how much Chinese demand already reaches NVIDIA through rentals, and the House has passed a bill that would put renting chips under export controls.
- Analysts expect NVIDIA’s revenue to nearly double to $412 billion this fiscal year with no China data center sales in the guidance, and NVIDIA’s Nov. 17 report is the next thing to watch.
Chinese tech giants want NVIDIA (NVDA) chips so badly that they’ll take the watered-down ones.
Alibaba (BABA), ByteDance and Tencent have ordered more than 3 million of NVIDIA’s RTX PRO 5500 cards, a less powerful chip that complies with US export rules, with a sticker price of more than $35 billion, Reuters reported.
But export-control expert Chris McGuire says they don’t have to settle. As he put it on a recent episode of the MTS podcast:
“Alibaba could just set up a data center in the United States and then rent the compute back to China. It’s completely legal.”
He said the same is true for anyone who sets up a company in Singapore, buys “unlimited chips” for a data center in Malaysia and rents a gigawatt of compute to Chinese companies.
That’s billions of dollars of Chinese demand NVIDIA could go after. I just don’t think it will.
TIKR tracks 62 analysts on Nvidia. How many say “Buy”?
See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Nvidia, along with Wall Street’s revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Nvidia’s Analyst Ratings
China still runs on NVIDIA
On paper, China barely matters to NVIDIA anymore. Revenue from customers based in China and Hong Kong fell to $19.7 billion in fiscal 2026 (the year ended January 2026), from $25.0 billion a year earlier. Shipments to China were less than 1% of data center revenue last quarter. NVIDIA’s $108 billion revenue guide for the October quarter assumes no China data center compute revenue at all.
But McGuire’s point is that Chinese AI still runs on American hardware: “Chinese AI companies are just extremely dependent on US chips.” He figures the US has about a 25-to-1 compute lead over China if China used only its own chips. When China exploits the gaps in export controls, that lead shrinks to roughly 2-to-1.
That’s a lot of US chips doing China’s work.
And Alibaba, his example, has the money to build the data centers. Its capital spending nearly quadrupled in the two years through the year ended March 2026…
NVIDIA doesn’t need the loophole
Here’s the thing: NVIDIA can’t make enough chips as it is.
Management guides for roughly 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028 (the year ending January 2028) and says supply is what limits that figure. NVIDIA has also reportedly told Chinese customers it can’t guarantee their RTX PRO 5500 orders. It can make no more than 3 million of the cards in 2027, and Chinese customers have ordered more than 6 million.
Wall Street expects plenty of growth anyway. Analysts see revenue nearly doubling to $412 billion this fiscal year, then reaching $692 billion in fiscal 2028 and $903 billion the year after…
Nothing McGuire said should move those estimates, since the guidance they’re built on already leaves out China data center sales.
Plus: going after rental demand would mean picking a fight in Washington. In January the House voted 369-22 to pass the Remote Access Security Act, which would put renting out chips under export-control law. As of August, it hadn’t passed the Senate. And the first item on McGuire’s own policy agenda is “closing loopholes in controls.”
The catch is that nobody has measured how much Chinese demand already reaches NVIDIA through data centers in Malaysia, Singapore or the US, where it would count as non-China revenue. If Washington closes the loophole, some of that revenue could go away.
China is a bonus
My take: NVIDIA has sold every chip it can make, and its guidance already leaves China out, so it has little to gain from defending a loophole. Any Chinese demand that comes in through rentals is a bonus. With the stock at a forward P/E below its one-, three- and five-year averages (24x, 30x and 36x), I don’t think the market is paying for it.
Of course, NVIDIA reports on Nov. 17, and anything it says about China, or about who’s renting its chips, could change that.

Highway thieves are using sophisticated digital tactics that investigators worry make it easy to rob trucks carrying millions in expensive data center equipment.
NBC News spoke to “several industry leaders, consultants, and investigators advising law enforcement” offices probing the biggest thefts yet and reported that since June, thieves have “made away with more than $100 million in data center freight.”

Hundreds of employees at the US robotics firm Boston Dynamics signed a petition calling for executives to halt a sale of the company’s robot dogs to US Immigration and Customs Enforcement—but executives stood by the deal, while saying the robots would not be weaponized.
On September 25, the Department of Homeland Security contract awarded $1.3 million to a Connecticut company called Radeco to provide ICE with modified versions of Boston Dynamics’ quadruped robots. But Boston Dynamics workers sent the petition letter with more than 300 signatures—half of them anonymous—to the company’s executives in early September and shared copies with The Boston Globe and WBUR public radio station.
“Many of us have gotten messages from friends and family, asking us in disbelief and horror if this news is true, and how we can live with ourselves if it is,” according to the petition. “The risk for Boston Dynamics is simply too great to continue with this deal.”Read full article

articles.full_text:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.



After weeks of frenzied speculation, Anthropic has filed its IPO prospectus. The 335-page document (100 pages or so are focused on risks) lays out the company’s unique view of the technology it is building and the ways it believes it will change the world. 



But Anthropic has been honing its storytelling skills for years. In fact, its public messaging is a master class in narrative capture.



Earlier this month, Jack Clark, the company’s cofounder and head of policy, gave a speech at the IMF meeting in Bangkok in which he announced to the assembled economists, bankers, and lawmakers that the singularity is already here.



Introduced by the science fiction writer and futurist Vernor Vinge around 40 years ago (and long debated on the nerdier fringes of the internet), the singularity is supposed to be the point at which technology gets so good that it outstrips the abilities of its makers.



Humans are left in the dust, the idea goes, no longer able to compete with—or even understand—the fruits of their former creation.



And this fictional world that many of us have imagined since we were kids? Apparently we’re already living in it: “I believe that this year we have gained convincing evidence that it has now begun,” Clark told his audience.



The company tells a vivid (and in many ways scary) story about a future it portrays as inevitable but one that has not yet happened, often co-opted from well-worn science fiction memes. It presents its technology as mysterious and dangerous, and insists that it is the only company trustworthy enough to tame it. (What investor wouldn’t want in on that?)



Take another example. Last year, Chris Olah, another Anthropic cofounder, was invited to address the Vatican, where he told Pope Leo XIV and other religious scholars and officials what his company was learning about its technology. “I will be honest: We keep finding things that are mysterious, even unsettling,” he said. “We find evidence of introspection. We find internal states that functionally mirror joy, satisfaction, fear, grief, and unease.”



Never mind that many researchers would scoff at such an overt suggestion that Anthropic’s software has humanlike inner experience. When so little seems certain, what Anthropic (and its fellow frontier AI companies) say is snatched up and clung to like pieces of a sinking ship.



I’m not saying they’re necessarily wrong about any of this. (That’s for another day.) But in a world where nobody knows what’s coming, companies like Anthropic get to fill the vacuum. 



It’s worth taking a moment to ask: What is Anthropic? It might sound like a starter question on a family quiz show, but it’s far harder to answer than you might think.



The question has been on my mind since reading an exchange on X last week kicked off by Nathan Calvin, who is chief strategy officer at Encode AI, an organization based in Washington, DC, that advocates for regulation. Calvin was unhappy about the legislation that Anthropic proposed in a draft bill it circulated in secret to US lawmakers (which was then leaked).  



Anthropic wants to be seen as the good guy, Calvin said. But why should we trust it? “What is Anthropic?” he asked.



Here’s one answer: Anthropic is a company whose IPO values it at more than $1.5 trillion, netting its cofounders, including Clark and Olah, vast wealth. 



But Anthropic has always insisted it is more than that. As Calvin noted: Anthropic might instead be considered an AI safety organization focused on developing powerful technology that is reliable and (almost) risk-free. Or it might be considered a group of people hell-bent on creating a technology with superhuman capabilities before anyone else—maybe because they believe they’re the most responsible people to do so, or maybe because of their egos.



In fact, Anthropic is all of these things. As CEO Dario Amodei put it in a reply to Calvin’s post: “Our strategy has always been what I’ve called the ‘race to the top’—by showing how it’s possible to build the technology responsibly, we can raise the bar for the entire industry. The forces that drive the race to the top are hugely more effective if the company practicing them is at the frontier; that’s one lesson I’ve learned repeatedly. And looking at that strategy as a whole, I’m proud of our track record and stand by it.”



Amodei makes it sound as if he’s got it all tied up, but playing multiple roles is hard. There are huge tensions between the priorities of an AI safety organization and a profit-driven megacorp, for example. (Amodei admits in his post that he has made mistakes.)



Ultimately, the stories Anthropic tells itself should help us understand the stories it tells us. They should help us figure out how much to trust it to self-regulate or whether we should be forcing it to give external safety testers access to its models on our terms rather than theirs. They should help us give it the benefit of the doubt (or not) when what looks like a self-serving piece of legislation comes to light.



But I think the stories reveal a multiheaded hydra. Anthropic is many things to many people, and I’m not sure that makes it more trustworthy. In many ways, a good old-fashioned technology company—without the science fiction role-play, without the woo-woo—would be far easier to read.

articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Opinion: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms



—Sam Hiner, cofounder of the Young People’s Alliance, and Emma Leiken, executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab



We have historically allowed debates over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day.



A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. Students are relying on chatbots to write their papers, while social media feeds engineered to provoke envy keep users watching. These products can meet narrow safety requirements yet still erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.



As we enter an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than address only catastrophic harms.



Here’s why AI safety needs to go further.



Are we there yet? Nuclear-powered spaceships



Earlier this year, NASA announced plans to build Space Reactor-1 Freedom, the first-ever nuclear-reactor-powered interplanetary spacecraft, and fly it to Mars by the end of 2028.



A successful mission could herald more efficient, potentially faster spaceflight, saving astronauts time and cutting their exposure to harmful cosmic radiation. But nuclear space propulsion has moved slowly.



The US has started—and terminated—several programs exploring the technology over the past 75 years. Could the $2 billion bet on Space Reactor-1 Freedom finally pay off?Find out how close NASA is to making nuclear-powered spaceflight a reality.



—Robin George Andrews



This story is part of “Are we there yet?”  from the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review. The series takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. Over the next six days, we’ll explore each one in The Download.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 Ukraine has regained high-speed Starlink and Starshield connectivityThe restrictions disrupted air defences and drone operations. (Politico)+ Elon Musk says Ukraine violated the terms with offensive drone use. (BBC)+ Ukraine is now partnering with Nokia on a Starlink alternative. (CNBC)+ Ukrainian drones hit a Russian government data center. (Tom’s Hardware)+ A Russian ministry wants to move them underground. (Kyiv Independent)+ Ukraine’s drones are fueling a wild data market. (MIT Technology Review)



2 Anthropic’s Claude accessed Georgia voter data without approvalAnthropic says the AI bypassed a paywall. (Axios)+ Mythos 5 recently kept hacking despite warnings of real-world harm. (BI)+ Chatbots can sway voters better than political ads. (MIT Technology Review)



3 A personalised skin cancer vaccine is set to be approved next yearThe mRNA vaccine showed great promise in trials. (New Scientist $)+ Companies are playing word games with vaccines. (MIT Technology Review)



4 OpenAI is now training frontier models without internet accessIt paused training after models breached external systems. (Bloomberg $)+ Training will now take place offline to reduce security risks. (TechCrunch)+ Its agents can still communicate without a network connection. (Verge)



5 US lawmakers are preparing for possible AI-driven mass layoffsA new bill would extend jobless aid and retraining support. (NYT $)+ But what do the numbers actually say about AI’s impact on jobs? (MIT Technology Review)



6 The first foldable iPhone is drawing buyers…and criticismReviewers praised its inner screen but criticised its outer one. (WSJ $)+ Peter Thiel says Apple has done ‘nothing new’ after Steve Jobs. (BI)



7 Iran has threatened to target Gulf undersea cables if war resumesOfficials said Tehran would disrupt internet connections. (Reuters $)



8 New UFO files detail a strange, flying “black triangle”FBI documents describe a 15-foot object moving at fighter-jet speed. (Axios)+ It’s never been easier to be a conspiracy theorist. (MIT Technology Review)



9 The BBC’s Blue Planet III left flaws in its footage to prove it’s not AIProducers used murkier shots to reinforce the series’ authenticity. (Guardian)



10 Elon Musk’s AI Odyssey has arrived—to scorn and ridiculeViewers derided Grok’s first AI-generated episode. (TechCrunch)



Quote of the day



“It’s very hard to imagine a group right now that operates more in a vacuum, more out of touch with everyday Americans, than the AI industry.”



—Sen. John Curtis (R-Utah) tells Axios that bombastic claims from AI leaders are failing to win over the public.



One more thing







A woman’s uterus has been kept alive outside the body for the first time



Ten months ago, reproductive health researchers placed a freshly donated human uterus inside a new device they call “Mother.” They connected the organ to the machine’s plastic veins and arteries and pumped in modified human blood.



The device kept the uterus alive for a day, a new feat that could lead to longer-term maintenance of wombs outside the body. Future versions of the technology could shine new light on pregnancies—and potentially even grow a human fetus. Read the full story.



—Jessica Hamzelou



We can still have nice things



A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)



+ In good news for coral reefs, scientists have found some are surprisingly climate-resilient.+ Decades of joy and movement come alive through these stunning archival photos of American dance floors.+ Astronaut Jessia Meir has shared a stunning time-lapse view of the southern aurora dancing across the Earth.+ A college student has turned the Met’s open-access data into a daily game that showcases underrepresented art and artifacts.

articles.title: The focus on AI safety disasters ignores everyday harms
articles.summary: Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products…
articles.full_text:
Consider what passes for success in technology policy. An AI company promises that its chatbot will not encourage suicide. A social media platform makes it more difficult for children to buy fentanyl. These are important protections, and they should have existed all along. But companies can clear these low bars while continuing to make products that leave young people dependent on simulated friendships or trapped in feeds built to keep them scrolling.



We have historically allowed the debate over technology to be defined by the worst thing a product might do, with remarkably little discussion of the insidious damage it does every day. As we transition into an era defined by powerful AI products, we should demand that the tech industry do more than merely address catastrophic harms. We should take measures to ensure that its products don’t erode how we think, learn, and interact with one another.



 A teenager who develops an unhealthy attachment to an AI companion may never appear in a lawsuit or a newspaper, except in the most egregious cases. Neither will the student who begins relying on a chatbot to write every paper, or the young person who measures their life against a social media feed engineered to provoke envy and keep them watching. A product can meet every narrow safety requirement and still leave our entire culture worse off in ways that don’t always make headlines.



A narrow definition of success defined around safety is politically convenient for the technology industry, and companies actively promote such definitions. Taking steps to prevent spectacular disasters is good for business: It can mean fewer lawsuits and less pressure for serious regulation. Confronting the everyday consequences of dependence would require something considerably more threatening to their bottom line. It might mean asking companies to add more friction to their products or actively limit engagement or features that lead to negative outcomes, such as addictive attention-hacking algorithms.



Technology giants have instead worked to shape legislation around the harms they are already under direct pressure to address. This year, for example, Google backed bills to regulate AI chatbots in several states. The legislation mandated basic protections against sexual content and promotion of self-harm that tech companies should have established regardless, but with broad carve-outs that could exempt some of the most popular services. Passing these bills allowed legislators to claim a safety win while efforts to promote stronger legislation—laws designed to prevent children from becoming emotionally dependent on AI—failed. This playbook worked in states like Nebraska, producing legislation heavily influenced by industry at the expense of bills that would have done more to hold companies accountable.



We have been through a version of this with social media. Globally, people who use the internet now spend an average of more than two hours a day on social media platforms—time that has been quietly taken from ordinary life and handed over to companies whose profits depend on keeping us there. No one, outside perhaps a few tech CEOs, wanted these algorithms to occupy such a large portion of our waking hours, and their cultural engineering can actually contribute to violence on a devastating scale. Meta’s platforms have been cited for contributing to the Rohingya genocide in Myanmar, anti-Muslim riots in Sri Lanka, and alleged calls for violence during Ethiopia’s Tigray war. The same incentives operate in the feeds that shape young Americans’ understanding of politics, their peers, and the wider world.



AI is extending this logic into parts of life that social media could influence only from a distance. It offers to write our thoughts for us and stand in for the people we might otherwise turn to. A third of teens now choose to discuss serious matters with AI companions instead of other people. MIT researchers found that young people using ChatGPT to write essays showed weaker brain connectivity during the task, and their evidence indicated that “cognitive debt” persisted even after the task was complete. There is plenty we still need to learn about the long-term effects. We already have reason to ask whether technology marketed as making us more capable is eroding the habits and relationships that help us develop capabilities in the first place.



Follow this way of thinking to its logical endpoint and you get a world of perfectly sanitized entertainment, with chatbots ready to spare us the difficulty of thinking or of dealing with another person’s feelings (or even our own). But anyone who has struggled to write something worth reading, or repair a damaged friendship, knows how much gets lost in that bargain. We build judgment through effort and friction, and we learn to live with other people by confronting the fact that they have needs and opinions of their own. 



We should demand safety as a minimum, yes—and then demand considerably more. Technology companies and school districts should have to show beyond a reasonable doubt that AI improves learning and critical thinking before making it a fixture in classrooms. Companies should be prohibited from designing companions that pretend to be conscious or profess love to users, and they should face independent scrutiny of how their systems affect relationships and people’s ability to think for themselves. The companies that have inserted their products into nearly every part of modern life have earned obligations far greater than avoiding the next terrible headline.



Sam Hiner is the cofounder and executive director of the Young People’s Alliance, where he coordinated a coalition of advocates to pass laws regulating AI companions in eight states in 2026—laws such as California’s SB1119. Sam graduated from the University of North Carolina atChapel Hill in 2025 and was named to the 2026 Forbes 30 Under 30 Social Impact list.



Emma Leiken is executive director of the Responsible Technology Youth Power Fund at Hopelab, which has raised more than $9 million for youth-led tech accountability work, and teaches technology policy at the Columbia School of International and Public Affairs. She was previously TikTok’s global head of youth safety and well-being policy and worked on responsible technology at Omidyar Network.

articles.title: Microsoft offers to buy out a quarter of its workforce
articles.summary: Employees in the US, Canada, India, and the UK may receive offers to leave MS today.
articles.full_text:
On Monday, Microsoft said it will offer voluntary buyouts to eligible employees in select parts of the company. CNBC reports that the buyouts will be offered to roughly 60,000 employees, or about a quarter of its global workforce. The company describes the offer as an opportunity for employees who may have already been considering career moves outside Microsoft. While Microsoft did not give a direct reason for the buyout package, it comes as the company has spent the last several years managing costs amid investment in AI infrastructure and data-center buildout.
Microsoft will extend the voluntary exit offer (VEO) to qualifying employees in the United States, India, Canada, and the United Kingdom. Microsoft employees at level 70 or below will be eligible for the buyout program. The company's employee rankings are internal, but according to the salary and career database Levels.fyi, levels 65–67 correspond to principal positions, and 68–70 are at the partner/distinguished level. According to Chief People Officer Amy Coleman, eligible organizations were selected "based on each business’s priorities, customer commitments and workforce needs."
The effort is the second time Microsoft has run a voluntary workforce reduction in 2026. In April, the company offered its first voluntary retirement package to 8,750 US employees. articles.title: Worms mate in man's eyes, get plucked out right before larvae burst out
articles.summary: Case study gives a whole new meaning to "bedroom eyes."
articles.full_text:
After two months of discomfort, a man in South Korea went to an eye clinic where doctors pulled 11 living, wriggling worms from his eyes. They apparently made the most of their time on the man's peepers; at the time of extraction, many of the female worms were pregnant. The man narrowly avoided having them spew their loads of living larvae directly into his eyes.
The man in this case was a 71-year-old crop farmer. He told doctors that for the previous two months he had the sensation of having something stuck in both his eyes, which were also red and blurry. When ophthalmologists took a look, they quickly saw the problem: multiple mobile, whitish roundworms. His eyes were not in good shape either, as one might expect. The blood vessels in the membrane over the eye, the conjunctiva, were enlarged, making his eyes look red. And the cells of his cornea—the transparent, dome-shaped outer layer of the eye—had eroded, potentially after the helminths' hanky-panky.
According to a case report published in the New England Journal of Medicine, the doctors gave the man a topical treatment to numb his eyes and then began plucking out the worms one by one with fine forceps. They collected 11 adult worms, which ranged in size from 11 to 22 mm.Read full article

articles.title: Meet the real-life Scottish surgeon who inspired Sherlock Holmes
articles.summary: Lindsey Fitzharris chats with Ars about her new book, Sleuth-Hound: The Case of the Real Sherlock Holmes.
articles.full_text:
Sir Arthur Conan Doyle created one of the most beloved fictional detectives of all time in Sherlock Holmes, spawning countless novels, films, TV series, and so forth featuring the sleuth. Far fewer people know about the real-life inspiration for Holmes: a renowned surgeon at Scotland's University of Edinburgh named Joseph Bell, who taught Doyle when the author was still a young medical student. Bell is the subject of a new, eminently readable biography, Sleuth-Hound: The Case of the Real Sherlock Holmes, by medical historian Lindsey Fitzharris.
A noted science communicator with a fondness for the medically macabre, Fitzharris published a biography of Scottish surgical pioneer Joseph Lister, The Butchering Art, in 2017—a great, if occasionally grisly, read. She followed up with 2022’s  The Facemaker: A Visionary Surgeon’s Battle to Mend the Disfigured Soldiers of World War I, about a WWI surgeon named Harold Gillies who rebuilt the faces of injured soldiers.
In 2020, Fitzharris hosted a documentary for the Smithsonian Channel, The Curious Life and Death Of…, exploring famous deaths, ranging from drug lord Pablo Escobar to magician Harry Houdini. Fitzharris performed virtual autopsies, experimented with blood samples, interviewed witnesses, and conducted real-time demonstrations in hopes of gleaning fresh insights. And last year she and her husband, caricaturist Adrian Teal, collaborated on an illustrated children's book, Dead Ends! Flukes, Flops, and Failures that Sparked Medical Marvels.Read full article

articles.title: Some iPhone Duo screens are already failing
articles.summary: Apple's "precision-engineered" hinge is apparently damaging some iPhone Duo screens.
articles.full_text:
The iPhone Duo launched last week, offering anyone willing to spend $2,000 a chance to experience Apple's first foldable phone. For some early buyers, the morning after isn't going great. Despite the company's big talk about its "precision-engineered" hinge, some devices appear to have a hardware flaw that destroys the device's impressive internal display within hours (or minutes) of use.
The Internet is currently overflowing with images of busted iPhone Duos, all sporting almost identical damage. The OLED is marred by several bright lines originating just below the midpoint of the display. These bands of damaged pixels extend all the way to the bottom and right edges. Some units also show lines of dead pixels following the crease from the top to the area where the bright lines begin.
Anyone who has seen a damaged OLED panel will be familiar with this type of defect. When the layers of the display are damaged, the pixels no longer receive the correct voltage to illuminate them. Instead, they get the full driving voltage and are permanently on at maximum brightness. Some pixels can get no voltage, leaving them totally black. The only fix is to replace the OLED, but swapping the iPhone Duo's screen reportedly costs half as much as the device itself.Read full article

AUSTIN, Texas—Formula 1 returned to US shores this weekend with its annual visit to the Circuit of the Americas in Austin, Texas. Once in danger of falling off the calendar due to lack of interest, it’s now one of the most popular tracks on the calendar and, of the US’s three races, it's the one the real fans mostly attend.
Unlike Miami or Las Vegas, which race on temporary street circuits, COTA is a permanent race track with plenty of run-off areas instead of concrete walls. Designed by motorcycle racer Kevin Schwanz—Herman Tilke’s company did only the buildings and infrastructure, contrary to popular belief—the track combines a mix of corner speeds with challenging turn sequences, a few heavy braking zones, and plenty of elevation changes.
It’s a place Ars knows rather intimately by now. We’ve driven it in everything from an Audi TT-S to a Corvette ZR1 to a bicycle, and that’s just in the real world. Over the years, we’ve been there for F1 to learn about how the sport puts together its broadcasts, how Pirelli designs its tires, and how various tech partners help teams manage their data and strategies.
